question: What makes a function easy to read and understand, and how should functions be sized, named, parameterised and structured?
contributions: A set of rules for functions: small, do one thing, one level of abstraction, stepdown rule, descriptive names, few arguments, no side effects, command-query separation, exceptions over error codes, DRY.

results.claim: Martin states functions should hardly ever reach 20 lines and that blocks inside if/while should be one line, ideally a call; this is his judgement, not research.
results.setup: Experience of one author over about four decades, Java examples; no study cited.
results.quote: Functions should hardly ever be 20 lines long.

results.claim: Martin concedes he has no research showing that very small functions are better.
results.setup: Opening of the 'Small!' section; basis is his own range of function sizes written (3,000-line, 100 to 300 lines, 20 to 30 lines).
results.quote: I can’t provide any references to research that shows that very small functions are better.

results.claim: Indent level inside a function should not exceed one or two.
results.setup: Consequence of one-line blocks; no data.
results.quote: the indent level of a function should not be greater than one or two.

results.claim: A worked example refactors the FitNesse testableHtml function (Listing 3-1) into a nine-line function (Listing 3-2), then a four-line one (Listing 3-3), then a class of small methods (Listing 3-7).
results.setup: Single Java function from FitNesse 20070619; no readability measurement, reader is asked to judge in three minutes.
results.quote: I was able to capture the intent of the function in the nine lines of Listing 3-2.

results.claim: A function does one thing if it does only steps one level of abstraction below its name; a second test is whether another function can be extracted whose name is not a restatement of its implementation.
results.setup: Definition of 'one thing' via the TO paragraph; reference [G34] in Chapter 17.
results.quote: If a function does only those steps that are one level below the stated name of the function, then the function is doing one thing.

results.claim: Ideal argument count is zero, then one, then two; three should be avoided and more than three needs very special justification.
results.setup: Rule of thumb; reasons given are reader load and combinatorial testing, with no data.
results.quote: Three arguments (triadic) should be avoided where possible.
results.note: Same page: 'More than three (polyadic) requires very special justification'.

results.claim: A boolean flag argument signals that a function does two things and should be split into two functions.
results.setup: Example render(true) vs renderForSuite() and renderForSingleTest(); Martin kept the flag in Listing 3-7 only to limit refactoring scope.
results.quote: We should have split the function into two: renderForSuite() and renderForSingleTest().

results.claim: Side effects are lies: checkPassword that also calls Session.initialize() creates a hidden temporal coupling.
Algorithm duplicated four times in Listing 3-1 (SetUp, SuiteSetUp, TearDown, SuiteTearDown) was collapsed into one include method.
results.quote: there is an algorithm that gets repeated four times, once for each of the SetUp, SuiteSetUp, TearDown, and SuiteTearDown cases.
results.note: Text wraps across lines in the PDF; quote joins them.

results.claim: Martin writes his functions long first, covered by unit tests, then refactors them to follow the rules; he does not write them that way to start.
results.setup: Personal process; the safety net is a unit test suite covering every clumsy line.
results.quote: I don’t write them that way to start. I don’t think anyone could.

limits: Martin states he has no research evidence that very small functions are better (p. 34); all rules rest on his experience.
Examples are Java and OO; several rules (switch via polymorphism and abstract factory, this as output argument, Error.java recompilation) depend on that setting and do not carry directly to Python.

The chapter says 'one thing' is hard to define and gives no way to tell when decomposition has gone too far; the over-decomposition and single-exit-return points are partly hedged ('every circumstance is unique', p. 39).
Flag-argument advice is applied unevenly: Listing 3-7 keeps render(pageData, boolean isSuite) by his own admission.
The chapter does not discuss comments; the note's page-54 comment quote comes from Chapter 4, not this PDF.
practices: Keep functions very small; blocks inside if/else/while should be one line, ideally a call (pp. 34-35).
Keep the indent level of a function to one or two (p. 35).
Make a function do one thing: only steps one level below its name; extract until you cannot pull out a function whose name is not a restatement (pp. 35-36).
A function divided into sections (declarations, initializations, sieve) is doing more than one thing (p. 36).
One level of abstraction per function; do not mix high-level calls with low-level string details (p. 36).
Order functions by the stepdown rule so the file reads as top-down TO paragraphs (p. 37).
Tolerate a switch only once, to create polymorphic objects, behind inheritance (pp. 37-39).
Use long descriptive names, prefer a long name to a short enigmatic one or a long comment, try several names, and use consistent phrasing (pp. 39-40).
Prefer zero, one or two arguments; avoid triads; wrap related arguments in an object (pp. 40-43).
Avoid output arguments; change the state of the owning object instead (p. 45).
Avoid flag arguments; split into two functions (p. 41).
Do not mix commands and queries: either change state or return information (pp. 45-46).
Prefer exceptions to returned error codes, extract try/catch bodies into functions, and make error handling the only thing such a function does (pp. 46-47).
Single-entry single-exit matters little in very small functions; multiple return, break or continue is acceptable, goto is not (pp. 48-49).
Write the first draft messy under a unit test suite, then refactor while keeping tests passing (p. 49).

terms.definition: FUNCTIONS SHOULD DO ONE THING. THEY SHOULD DO IT WELL. THEY SHOULD DO IT ONLY.
A brief description of a function as steps one level of abstraction below its name, in the style of LOGO's TO keyword.
Every function is followed by those at the next level of abstraction so the program reads top-down, descending one level at a time.
Functions with zero, one, two, three, or more than three arguments.
A boolean passed into a function; it announces that the function does one thing if true and another if false.
A hidden thing a function does beyond what its name promises, such as changing class variables, parameters or globals; often causes temporal coupling.
A function that can only be called at certain times, for example when it is safe to initialize the session.
Functions should either do something or answer something, but not both.
A class such as an Error enum that many other classes must import, so changing it forces recompilation and redeployment.
